effects.log: You keep the ash in a jar on the high shelf. It is a poor sort of trophy.

choices.text: Scatter the ash on the wind

effects.log: You scatter it from the temple steps. The wind takes it in without a sound.

events.text: The chain loosened in the night, and {bd7_name} woke clear-eyed for the first time in years, looked at you, and understood everything. {bd7_He} has already gone, and left the door open, and a line on the altar: a date and a name, a promise of what is to come.

effects.log: You read it three times. The name is yours.
You burn it. That does not make it less true.

events.text: The chain gave way while you were at the Court of the Twelve. {bd7_name} is gone, and the Court has been told. By evening a summons arrives at your temple gate with the Court's seal.

choices.text: Answer the summons with a straight face

effects.log: You go. You answer each question in the same short, plain way. It earns you a small bad name and not a large one.

choices.text: Withdraw into the temple for a season

effects.log: You withdraw for a season until the summons is forgotten, or at least misfiled.

events.text: The chain failed, and {bd7_name} is gone, and this time went to the Heavenly Court with the whole of it: the vault, the link, your name. Gods turn their heads in the Hall of Offerings as you walk past, and cheerful ones stop speaking.

effects.log: You walk the length of the hall with your back straight. A few gods nod. A few do not.
You keep to your altar for a season. It is not a courageous thing, but it is quiet.

events.text: You draw the last link of the Vow-Chain from {bd7_name} on a clear morning. The silver comes away like a thread of rain from a leaf. {bd7_He} stands very still for some time. Then {bd7_he} looks at you, as at a stranger, which is what you now are.

effects.log: You say it plainly. {bd7_name} does not answer. The silence has weight.

choices.text: Give {bd7_him} an offering for the road

effects.log: You give a sheaf of offerings. {bd7_name} takes them and goes, and the temple is a little less warm.

events.text: The chain is off {bd7_name} now, and the lamps in your temple burn a little steadier. {bd7_He} stays one more night, politely, to be sure it is real, and in the morning bows and goes down the steps one at a time.

effects.log: You watch until the mist takes {bd7_him}. Something in you lets out a long breath.
You call a name. {bd7_name} does not turn. That is its own answer.

events.text: You release {bd7_name} on the anniversary of the first link, with a scribe of the Book of Fates to witness, and a line is struck out in the vault. It costs you nothing but ink. It costs you everything else you were proud of.

choices.text: Sign your own name beneath the strike

effects.log: You sign. The Book will remember it longer than you will.
You say it was nothing. Nobody who knows you believes it.

events.text: The Heavenly Court sends a scribe to your altar with a question in a bronze tube: whether a certain chain was ever drawn from the lower vault of the Book of Fates, and by whom. A god of the Silent Drum watches you read. The scribe watches your face.

effects.log: You say it was you. The scribe writes it down without surprise, and the Court does not press the matter further than a rebuke.
You deny it. The scribe bows and goes, but the god of the Drum does not look away from your hands for a long time.

choices.text: Name another god as the thief

effects.log: You point to a rival with a straight face. The scribe takes the name, and you take the cost of it with you.

events.text: A prayer comes up in the night from a mortal world, and it is not a prayer to you: a retainer of another god kneels before a half-melted silver chain, naming the god who forged it. The Book of Fates has already written your name beside it.

choices.text: Go to the Court and confess

effects.log: You go. The Court listens, sighs, and writes a short entry that will be read for ten thousand years.

choices.text: Go and say it was not you

effects.log: You go and lie, with a calm face. The Court lets it stand, for now.
You give them a name. The Court writes it with a slow, careful hand.

events.text: Someone left a silver link on your altar overnight, with no note. Nobody has to say what it means. By noon the pantheons know, and the lesser gods turn their faces as you pass.

effects.log: You say, loudly, in the Hall of Offerings, that it is yours. Silence. Then, slowly, talk again.
You deny it with heat. The heat is the giveaway, but the gods are polite.

choices.text: Say a former ally left it

effects.log: You say a former ally left it. The gods nod, and some even believe it.

events.text: The new priest of your temple, {dv7_name}, sweeps the steps at dawn and talks to you while sweeping, half a prayer and half a complaint about the pigeons. You have heard ten thousand prayers. This is the first that made you want to answer in words.

choices.text: Answer in a dream that night

effects.log: You answer in a dream, one line, and {dv7_name} wakes laughing and says so to the pigeons.

choices.text: Keep the silence a god is supposed to keep

effects.log: You keep the silence. The prayer goes up, unanswered, and returns in the morning a little quieter.

choices.text: Send a feather as a sign

effects.log: A white feather lies on the swept step. {dv7_name} looks at it a long time, then at the sky.

events.text: On the night of the first rains the temple roof leaks, and you watch {dv7_name} climb the ladder with a bucket and a lantern, talking to you the whole time as if you were holding the ladder. You are, in a way. A god's hand is steady when it is wanted.

choices.text: Steady the ladder with a breath of wind

effects.log: You steady it. {dv7_name} stops, looks about, and says, "Thank you," to the empty air, which is entirely right.

choices.text: Do nothing, as the Book of Fates says

effects.log: You do nothing, as the Book says. {dv7_name} finishes the roof alone, soaked and unthanked.

choices.text: Stop the rain over the roof alone

effects.log: You stop the rain over the roof, only there. {dv7_name} laughs, and tells no one.

events.text: A priest who is not afraid of you is rare. {dv7_name} arrives at your temple with a satchel of grain, a list of questions, and a polite refusal to kneel. "I will kneel," {dv7_he} says, "when I know who I am kneeling to."

choices.text: Show {dv7_him} the true shape of your domain

effects.log: You show {dv7_him}. {dv7_name} does not kneel, but stands very still, and then bows from the waist, like a person to a person.
You strike them dark. {dv7_name} lights them again with a flint, saying nothing, and kneels at last.
You laugh. The satchel is put down on the altar, and the questions begin.

events.text: Among the thousand voices that rise to your altar each night, one is hoarse, ill, and utterly honest. It is {dv7_name}, newly ordained, praying to a god of this domain out of a duty that is plain to hear, with a single line that is not duty. The line is, "Please be kind."

effects.log: You be kind. The next morning there is bread on the altar that the temple cannot afford, and {dv7_name} sleeping on the porch.
You remain distant. The prayer is heard and set down among the thousand, like any other.

choices.text: Listen for a year before answering

effects.log: You listen for a year. The line comes every night, and it changes you a little.

events.text: You come to the temple when the incense has burned down, in the shape of a plain traveller at the altar rail. {dv7_name} has set out two cups of hot barley tea and does not pretend to be surprised. The Book of Fates has a clause about this, you recall. You do not recall it hard.

choices.text: Sit and talk until the lamps gutter

effects.log: You sit and talk until the lamps gutter. {dv7_name} falls asleep mid-sentence with a hand on the rail.

choices.text: Make sure no angel of the Court is watching

effects.log: You send out a quiet hush over the courtyard. No angel is watching, tonight.

choices.text: Take {dv7_him} to the roof of the world for an hour

effects.log: You take {dv7_him} to the roof of the world, where the stars of your domain wheel slowly. {dv7_name} says nothing for a long time.
You do not come tonight. The tea goes cold, and {dv7_name} drinks it anyway.

events.text: {dv7_name} is ill with a winter cough that no healer-priest can lift. You stand at the foot of the sickbed in the guise of a pilgrim and cannot touch the fever without leaving a god's mark on the Book. The cough is a plain thing, and a plain thing can be a real danger to the mortal it takes.

choices.text: Lift the fever, mark or no mark

effects.log: You lift it. A thread of gold shows in the sickroom air for a moment, and the Book of Fates notes it somewhere far away.
You nurse {dv7_him} as a mortal would, with broth and honey. It takes three weeks, and the Court never knows.

choices.text: Ask a healing god of the Laughing River to look in

effects.log: You ask a healer of the Laughing River to look in, with a good lie to cover it. The cough lifts, and the healer's eyes are sharp.

choices.text: Withdraw and let the fever take its course

effects.log: You withdraw. It is the correct thing for a god. It is not a thing you forgive yourself.

events.text: The Court has put a new scribe in the clouds above your temple, a young angel with a quill and a fondness for the word "irregularity". {dv7_name} suggests a different hour for your meetings: the hour between the evening and the morning prayer, which the Book of Fates leaves unwritten.

effects.log: You meet in the unwritten hour. The scribe's quill finds nothing to record, and you and {dv7_name} share a thin flask of spiced tea.

choices.text: Come only on the nights of fog

effects.log: You come only in fog. Meetings are rarer, safer, and lonelier.

choices.text: Come in daylight, as the god of the temple

effects.log: You walk into the temple at noon, openly, and bless the offerings. The scribe's quill moves very fast.
You stay away. The scribe leaves, bored.

events.text: {dv7_name} leaves you a gift at the altar each year: a clay cup, a knotted cord, a bundle of dried mint. This year it is a paper lamp. "For when the temple is dark," {dv7_he} writes on the paper, and you read it a dozen times before dawn.

choices.text: Light the lamp in your inner shrine

effects.log: You light the lamp. It burns with a small, honest flame, unlike any divine fire.

choices.text: Hide it in an unwritten page

effects.log: You hide it in an unwritten page of the Book of Fates, where no scribe will read.

choices.text: Hang it over the temple door

effects.log: You hang it over the temple door. The whole parish sees it, and thinks it a blessing.
You leave it unlit. A god ought not to want such things, and you want it too much.

events.text: During the Feast of Lamps the whole village packs the temple court, and you stand in the crush as a nobody, a hand's breadth from {dv7_name}, who is leading the chant. {dv7_He} sees you. {dv7_His} voice does not waver, and your name is in the next line of the hymn.

effects.log: You join in, quietly, among the others. Your voice carries a little, and the lamps flare.

choices.text: Slip out before the last verse

effects.log: You slip out before the last verse, and find a message tucked into your sleeve later.

choices.text: Cross the court and take {dv7_his} hand

effects.log: You cross the court in front of everyone and take {dv7_his} hand. The chant stumbles, then resumes louder.
You pretend not to know {dv7_him}. It is a poor trick, and {dv7_name} plays along.

events.text: A decade of nights. {dv7_name} is thirty-nine and has the first grey at the temples, and you notice, one evening, that you have been counting the years on {dv7_his} face as if it were a calendar. The word "mortal" sits in the temple like an extra guest.

effects.log: You say it, and know you are promising only for as long as {dv7_he} can pray.

choices.text: Change the subject to the harvest

effects.log: You change the subject. {dv7_name} lets you, carefully.

choices.text: Speak of what it is to be a god

effects.log: You speak of it all: the long dark, the weight of prayers. {dv7_name} listens and holds your hand tighter.
You withdraw for the year. The distance is a kind of mercy, you tell yourself.

events.text: At the end of the longest night of the year, when every lamp but one has gone out, you stand in the light of the one and say what a god may not say to a priest. {dv7_name} sets down the taper, turns, and for once has no pleasantry at all.

effects.log: You say it. {dv7_name} says it back, voice shaking. The words go up through the roof and nothing answers but the wind.

choices.text: Say it was only the lamp

effects.log: You say it was only the lamp talking, and the lie costs you something. {dv7_name} nods slowly, as if hearing a verdict.

events.text: {dv7_name} asks, at the foot of the altar, whether the gods ever grow lonely. It is asked simply, as one asks about the weather. "Yes," you say through the fire. "Of this, among other things." That is the whole confession.

effects.log: You say it. {dv7_name} takes your hand across the altar rail, and the fire burns a clear, steady gold.
You deflect, and vanish. The altar rail is still warm where {dv7_his} hand lay.

events.text: Under the temple bell, in the moment after the last stroke has faded, {dv7_name} says it first: "I know what you are. I am not afraid." {dv7_He} has known for years. It was only waiting for you.

effects.log: You tell {dv7_him}. {dv7_name} laughs, once, wetly, and holds on.
You tell {dv7_him} it cannot be. {dv7_name} says, "Then say it and look at me." You cannot.

events.text: A white-robed angel of the Heavenly Court appears in the temple court at noon with a scroll in a lacquer tube. It is addressed to you, and it contains the name of a village, the name {dv7_name}, and a record of every night you came in the guise of a traveller. The seal is the Court's, and it is not unkind.

effects.log: You read it to the end. It is thorough, and courteous, and there is nothing in it you can dispute.

choices.text: Burn it, and go down at once

effects.log: You burn it and go down to the temple that night. The roof is already watched.

events.text: A god of the Long Tide, in no hurry, mentions at a council that the Court has been asking after a certain small temple and its priest. "A small place," the god says. "Easily forgotten." The offering-wine is suddenly sour.

effects.log: You leave early, with a very civil face. The god of the Long Tide watches you go and does not finish the wine.
You ask, and they tell you, and every part of it is worse than you thought.

events.text: It is out. The Book of Fates has a new line in the margin: a god and a mortal priest, met three hundred times in the unwritten hour. The pantheons have been talking about little else for a week, and the lesser gods say "scandal" with an air of relief.

choices.text: Walk through the talk with your head up

effects.log: You walk through the council, and the talk dies as you pass and rises behind you.

choices.text: Stay in your temple for a season

effects.log: You stay in your temple for a season. The talk grows, as talk does, in the dark.

events.text: The Heavenly Court summons you to the Court of the Twelve. The presiding god reads from the Book of Fates without once looking up: 'The Book forbids a god and a mortal priest. Sever the tie by the new moon, or be struck from your seat.' Behind the god, the guard of the Court stands in a row.

choices.text: Marry in secret, and keep it hidden

effects.log: You say you will end it. You go down that night and wed {dv7_name} before a hearth-goddess who asks nothing.

ok.log: You stand in the Court of the Twelve and refuse. The Court, to everyone's surprise, flinches first.

fail.log: You stand in the Court of the Twelve and refuse. The Court does not flinch.

choices.text: Raise {dv7_him} to a lamp-god of your temple

effects.log: You carry the priest's name to the lower vault and ask for a lamp, a single small lamp. The scribe writes it, and does not look up.
You agree to end it. The presiding god nods, and a scribe writes your name in a thin hand.

events.text: Unmyeong, the god of fate, sends a messenger, not the Court, with a single knotted thread and a smile: end the matter, and the thread is cut. Keep it, and the Book remembers. A week later the Court sends a messenger of its own, and he is not smiling.

choices.text: Wed in secret, under a borrowed name

effects.log: You and {dv7_name} are wed by a hearth with the name of a dead acquaintance on the paper. Both messengers are left to guess.

ok.log: You send both messengers away in the same hour. The pantheons remember it as the day the Court blinked.

fail.log: You refuse them both. Neither of them is impressed.

choices.text: Raise {dv7_him} on a forged line in the Book

effects.log: You forge a line over a night, and in the morning you walk {dv7_name} into the Hall as a lamp-god of a far temple.

choices.text: Take the cut thread and end it

effects.log: You take the cut thread. It is cold, and it is light, and you never look at it again.

events.text: The marriage was found. The Court returns with the register of the hearth-goddess, the false name, and a page with your hand on it. The presiding god reads aloud: 'A second summons. There will not be a third.'

effects.log: You hide it better. The temple is moved quietly to a far valley of a far world, and {dv7_name} goes with it.

choices.text: Defy the Court to its face

ok.log: You defy them in the Court of the Twelve again, and this time the presiding god bows, a little, with a hard face.

fail.log: You defy them. The Court of the Twelve has been waiting for this.

choices.text: Raise {dv7_him} to a lamp-god in earnest

effects.log: You spend the last of your standing on a single small lamp, and go down for {dv7_name}.
You give {dv7_him} up. It is the second time, and it does not get easier.

events.text: A white bird lands on your altar with a rolled order: the mortal {dv7_name} is to be struck from the prayers of your temple, and you from your seat, unless the tie is ended by the turn of the season. The order is signed in three hands.

choices.text: Wed {dv7_him} in secret before the season ends

effects.log: You go down in a plain robe and wed {dv7_him} at the shrine of a river-god who asks no questions.

choices.text: Stand before the three and say no

ok.log: You say no in three ways to three signatures. The order is withdrawn with a polite sigh.

fail.log: You say no. The three signatories look at one another, and you realize you have been outvoted.

choices.text: Make {dv7_him} a lamp-god of your temple

effects.log: You make {dv7_name} a lamp-god, and the first flame of {dv7_his} divinity lights the temple, gold and trembling.
You let {dv7_him} go. It is the right thing, and it is a terrible thing, and both are true.

events.text: You and {dv7_name} are wed at a hearth in the corner of the temple, with a cat, a baker and a very old woman as witnesses, and nobody else. The vow is quick. The barley tea is hot. For a moment the whole Book of Fates is only a dusty book on a distant shelf.

effects.log: You toast the cat, and the cat does not mind, and {dv7_name} holds your hand and hides a grin in your sleeve.
You burn the paper afterward. The ashes smell of cedar, and the secret is safe, for now.

events.text: The Court gives a feast, an actual feast, in your honour: lamps, birds, a table for the Twelve. The scribes sit in the second row, stony. {dv7_name} walks into the Hall on your arm in a robe cut by hand, and no one stops {dv7_him}. It is the strangest sight the pantheons have seen in an age.

choices.text: Take {dv7_his} hand at the Court doors

effects.log: You take {dv7_his} hand. The lamps flare all at once, and the feast begins.

choices.text: Bow to the presiding god, lightly

effects.log: You bow lightly. The presiding god bows back, less lightly, and the Hall lets out a breath.

events.text: In the lower vault a scribe writes a new line into the Book of Fates, and the line holds. {dv7_name} stands beside you, a lamp-god now, blinking in the gold of {dv7_his} own new light. The temple does not know the difference, and neither, quite yet, do you.

effects.log: You show {dv7_him} every hall, every wheel of stars. {dv7_name} walks as if the floor might fall.

choices.text: Sit down together on the altar step

effects.log: You sit down together on the altar step, and neither of you says a word for an hour.

events.text: The two of you share a small shrine at the back of the temple, with a view of nothing but incense-smoke and a lamp that hums. {dv7_name} still leaves tea-leaves on the altar rail, and you still pretend not to mind. Whatever the Court calls it, the shrine is full of ordinary days.

choices.text: Plant a mint-bed in the court

effects.log: You plant a mint-bed, for the smell. It rises through the stones in the evening wind, thin and sweet.
You do nothing at all, together, for a whole afternoon. It may be the best afternoon of the age.

events.text: The Court does not kill. It sends two scribes in white, with a bowl of still water and a quiet voice. {dv7_name} is led out of the temple, memory washed, into exile in a village that is not {dv7_his} own, and you are told it is a mercy. No one dies. That is the Court's pride.

choices.text: Watch the road until it is empty

effects.log: You watch the road until it is empty. Nobody tells you to look away.

choices.text: Go to the new village anyway

effects.log: You go. The one who looks up from the well does not know your face. You buy a cup of water and say nothing.

events.text: They struck your name from the Court's rolls in front of the Twelve. {dv7_name} is sent away to a far world, and the shrine of your temple is shut with three ribbons of grey. You are left with your seat, which is smaller than it was, and your memory, which is not.

effects.log: You take it in silence. There is nothing else to take.

choices.text: Write one prayer and burn it

effects.log: You write one prayer. You burn it, and the smoke goes down toward the world where no one will answer.

events.text: Of all that the Court took, the hardest is the small things: the clay cup on the altar, the paper lamp in the drawer, the sound of {dv7_name}'s name. A scribe comes to collect them. You hand over the cup and keep the lamp.

effects.log: You keep the paper lamp, hidden in an unwritten page, where the Court does not look.
You give up everything, and the scribe looks almost sorry.

events.text: You end it in the first frost of the year, at the altar rail, with the last lamp burning. {dv7_name} listens without arguing, and thanks you for the years in a voice that is entirely level. You are halfway up the clouds before you find that you are weeping.

effects.log: You do not look back. You cannot be sure whether this is strength.

choices.text: Go back and say one last thing

effects.log: You go back. You say the one last thing. It does not change anything, but it is said.

events.text: It was the Court's doing, in the end. {dv7_name} is gone from the temple before you can reach it; the altar is cold, the cup is washed, and the neighbours say the priest was called away in the night. A white ribbon is knotted on the gate. You do not need it explained.

choices.text: Search the neighbouring worlds for a season

effects.log: You search for a season and find nothing. The worlds are many, and a mortal life moves quickly.
You let it be. It was never entirely yours to keep.

events.text: You end it on a cold morning, with a pot of warm tea and the temple bell sounding the hour. {dv7_name} walks the first half of the courtyard with you in silence and then stops. "Go on," {dv7_he} says. "It is a long way up."

effects.log: You go on. The road is long, and every step of it is clear.
You walk back with {dv7_him} as far as the first door, and say nothing at all.

events.text: In the third year of the secret, {dv7_name} leaves a pot of honeyed barley on the altar and does not say it is for you. You eat it with your fingers. Somewhere above, the Court stays patient, the way a cat stays patient at a hole.

choices.text: Keep a jar for the winter

effects.log: You keep a jar for the winter, in a high cupboard of your temple, and open it in the dark.

choices.text: Leave a feather on the altar in return

effects.log: You leave a white feather. It is the smallest sign a god can give, and it is read at once.

events.text: The pantheons have grown used to the mortal-born lamp in the temple. They call {dv7_name} 'the keeper', affectionately, because {dv7_he} lights the lamps before anyone asks. Even the presiding god of the Court once asked after {dv7_his} health, and flushed to be seen asking.

effects.log: You light the lamps together, from the first hall to the last, and it takes all evening.

choices.text: Invite the Twelve to the lamp-lighting

effects.log: You invite the Twelve to the lighting, and three of them come. It is a small victory, and you take it.

events.text: {dv7_name} has to learn how to be a god the way one learns to walk in a boat. The first century is balance. The second, patience. You answer every question patiently, and {dv7_he} writes the answers on temple paper and loses them, and you write them out again.

choices.text: Teach {dv7_him} a prayer-song of the domain

effects.log: You teach {dv7_him} slowly. {dv7_He} sings it in a priest's heavy voice, and it sounds better for it.

choices.text: Take {dv7_him} to hear the prayers rising

effects.log: You take {dv7_him} to the Gallery of Prayers. {dv7_He} listens for a long time, and does not speak.

events.text: Years later, a small bell sounds at the temple gate, and a stranger comes up the steps with a lamp. For one moment the walk is so like {dv7_name}'s that your heart stops. It is not. It is a pilgrim with a lamp.

effects.log: You offer the pilgrim tea. They sit with you for an hour and ask nothing, and it is the kindest thing of the year.

choices.text: Close the gate on the pilgrim

effects.log: You close the gate. The lamp goes up the steps regardless, and you do not look.

events.text: Of the secret, a dull ache remains: that there is one fewer person in the worlds who knows how your hand feels in the dark. You keep the ache anyway, the way you keep an old robe.

choices.text: Go down for the spring festival

effects.log: You go down in a plain robe for the spring festival, and stand in the crowd, unrecognised.
You stay in the temple. The festival goes on without you, as festivals do.

events.text: The two of you sit on the roof of the temple and watch the lights of the lower worlds go out one by one. {dv7_name} says, quite suddenly, "I used to think heaven was empty." "It is," you say. "But it is ours."

choices.text: Stay until the stars come out

effects.log: You stay until the stars come out, and then a while longer.
You fall asleep on the roof with a cloak over you both, and wake with frost in your hair.

events.text: {dv7_name} finds a white hair in the polished bronze and holds it up to the lamp like a thread from a weaver. "Look," {dv7_he} says, grinning. "The first of my many ranks." You laugh, and your laugh catches in the middle.

effects.log: You pluck it for luck, and keep it in a lacquer box. A small superstition, as good as any.
You say nothing, and kiss {dv7_him} on the forehead. It is the answer.

events.text: The years show in the way {dv7_name} climbs the temple steps now: a hand to the rail, a pause on the landing. You slow your steps to match, and neither of you says why. Gods outlive three generations of priests, and no one in the pantheons thinks about it at all.

effects.log: You carry {dv7_him} the last flight, and {dv7_he} grumbles about it, and holds on.
You sit with {dv7_him} on the landing, and listen to the prayers of the valley rise.

events.text: At the harvest festival a child asks if the old priest is some sort of grandparent to you. {dv7_name} laughs so hard that {dv7_he} has to sit down. You do not laugh. You have never seen the gap so clearly.

effects.log: You take {dv7_him} home early. {dv7_name} falls asleep in the chair with the lamp still lit.

choices.text: Say you are proud to be asked

effects.log: You say you are proud to be asked. The child gives you a honey-cake, which you eat very slowly.

events.text: Every year you bring a gift out of your domain, and every year there are fewer things {dv7_name} can use. This year it is a cushion, stuffed with the down of a dawn-bird. "For my knees," {dv7_he} says, and is too pleased to tease you. You have never been so aware of how much time is gone.

effects.log: You sit on the floor beside {dv7_him}, and {dv7_he} puts a hand on your head as if you were the old one.

choices.text: Say you will find a remedy

effects.log: You say you will find a remedy, and spend three nights in the vaults of the Book looking. You find nothing.

events.text: {dv7_name} dies in the spring, in an ordinary bed in the priest's quarters, with the shutters open and the sound of the temple bell. You are holding {dv7_his} hand when the breathing changes, and then it is only quiet. Below the window the village goes on with its morning prayers.

effects.log: You stay until the burial, and plant a mint-bed on the hill. It is small, and you water it every day for a year.

choices.text: Go back to your seat at once

effects.log: You go back at once, because you cannot bear the quiet. Your seat is quieter.

events.text: The temple bell tolls a long time for {dv7_name}. People come with rice cakes and paper offerings, and you thank each one, and none of them knows who you are. That night you light a paper lamp on the river. It floats a long way before it sinks.

choices.text: Light a second lamp for the years to come

effects.log: You light a second lamp, for the years you will still have. It is a long sum.
You sit at the altar alone, and the lamp on its hook flickers once, softly, in the draught.

events.text: {dv7_name}'s last words are about the lamp-oil, and whether you remembered to trim the wick. They are such ordinary words that for a long time afterward you cannot tell if the sorrow is big or small. In the end you decide it is both.

effects.log: You keep the lamp. It never burns quite right again.
You trim the wick. In the dark, the temple is almost bearable.

events.text: {bt7_name} and you swore friendship before the Book of Fates, a thousand years ago, on the day you both took your seats. The oath is in the margin, in two hands. Lately {bt7_name} has taken to leaving the Hall of the Twelve a moment before you speak, and returning a moment after.
events.arc: The God Who Broke a Vow

effects.log: You follow {bt7_him}, at a distance, to the door of a Lineage that has no love for you. {bt7_name} goes in, and does not look back.
You renew the oath aloud, in the empty Hall. {bt7_name} repeats it, one beat late, and the margin of the Book stays unmoved.

choices.text: Tell yourself it is the stars

effects.log: You tell yourself it is the stars. The stars, for once, have nothing to say.

events.text: A prayer meant for you reaches {bt7_name} first. You can tell, because the prayer-mortal's next offering is a little thinner, and {bt7_name}'s altar a little brighter. A friend who answers your prayers has either stolen from you or been very kind.
events.arc: The God Who Broke a Vow

choices.text: Count the offerings for a season

effects.log: You count them for a season. The sum is not kind.
You ask. {bt7_name} says it was a mistake of the Gallery, and offers a cup, and you drink it.

choices.text: Say nothing, and keep your own altar well

effects.log: You say nothing and attend your own altar twice as closely. The prayers return, slowly.

events.text: At the feast of the Twelve, {bt7_name} sits two seats from you, which is far, and next to a god of the Silent Drum, which is farther. The Silent Drum does not seat anyone next to it by chance. It watches you over the rim of a cup.
events.arc: The God Who Broke a Vow

choices.text: Watch the two of them for the evening

effects.log: You watch for the evening. They speak little, and exchange a dried fig, which tells you more than speech would.

choices.text: Cross the Hall and sit beside {bt7_him}

effects.log: You cross the Hall and sit beside {bt7_him}. The Drum smiles, and finishes the cup, and says nothing.
You leave early. The corridor is long and has a lot of doors.

events.text: The Book of Fates, which never lies, has a line smudged in the margin where your oath with {bt7_name} was written. A scribe says it was a spill of ink. The spill is in the shape of a hand, pressing out the word 'ever'.
events.arc: The God Who Broke a Vow

effects.log: You say nothing to the scribe, and begin to keep a sharper eye on {bt7_him}.

choices.text: Go to {bt7_him} with the smudged line

effects.log: You go to {bt7_him} with the page. {bt7_name} says, "I was going to tell you," and does not.
You re-ink it yourself, in a steady hand. The word 'ever' looks different in your writing.

events.text: At the {bt7_where}, with the gods of four pantheons in their seats and the scribes of the Book at their desks, {bt7_name} stands and says before all that the oath of friendship was never sworn in good faith. You were watching for it. You are on your feet before the last word.
events.arc: The God Who Broke a Vow

choices.text: Turn the charge back on {bt7_him} there and then

ok.log: You read, from the margin, the clause {bt7_name} signed in a different hand. The Court turns its head like a field of reeds.

fail.log: You open your mouth to answer and the words do not come in time. The silence is {bt7_his}.

effects.log: You endure it in silence, back straight, and let the Court whisper to itself.

events.text: {bt7_name} has chosen the moment well: after the third reading, with the scribes tired and the god of fate half asleep. In a clear voice at the {bt7_where}, {bt7_he} lays out the old secret of your domain that you told only {bt7_him}. You saw the weakness in the plan a month ago.
events.arc: The God Who Broke a Vow

choices.text: Answer in front of the whole Court

ok.log: You answer with the date of {bt7_his} own bargain with the Drum. The scribes' pens stop all at once.

fail.log: You answer, and the answer is not enough. A lamp gutters, somewhere, with a very small noise.

choices.text: Say nothing and bow your head

effects.log: You bow your head. It is the most difficult silence you have ever kept.

events.text: At the {bt7_where}, {bt7_name} bows to the presiding god and lays a sealed scroll on the table: a page of your private vow-ledger, in your hand. The presiding god reads it aloud. You knew this was coming, and still the Hall goes small.
events.arc: The God Who Broke a Vow

choices.text: Counter with the Drum's own letters

ok.log: You draw the letters from your sleeve and read the first line. The god of the Drum leaves before the third.

fail.log: You draw the letters, and they are the wrong ones. The presiding god smiles faintly.

choices.text: Let the scroll be read to the end

effects.log: You let it be read to the end, with your hands in your lap. It is not a long scroll, as scrolls go.

events.text: You never saw it coming. At the {bt7_where}, with the gods of the Court in their seats and the Book open on its stand, {bt7_name} sets down a cup, smiles at you, and tells the Court what you did in the War in Heaven. It is true, and nobody had known it but one friend.
events.arc: The God Who Broke a Vow

choices.text: Bow your head and say it is true

effects.log: You say it is true. It is a small, plain voice, and the Court, to its own surprise, quiets.
You rise and leave, with a bow to the presiding god, and the doors close behind you softly.

events.text: Someone has sold your name to the Lineage of the Hidden Star, and the proof is on the table of the {bt7_where} for every god to pass hand to hand. The hand that wrote it was {bt7_name}'s. You were told, once, that a broken vow makes a sound. It does not. It makes a silence.
events.arc: The God Who Broke a Vow

choices.text: Take the paper and read it calmly

effects.log: You take the paper and read it calmly, to the last line, and pass it on. The Court cannot decide what you are.
You leave it unread and finish your cup. A page can only wound someone who lets it.

events.text: The Court of Vows is over. The scribes have gone back to their desks. Whatever else, {bt7_name} broke the oath, and you were there to see it written, and a thousand years of the pantheons will remember both. You sit on the steps of the Hall at dawn, and decide what the rest of the story is.
events.arc: The God Who Broke a Vow

effects.log: You plan it, patiently, over a century, as the gods do everything.
You forgive {bt7_him}, in your own temple, with no one watching. It is lighter than you expected.
You strike {bt7_him} from your page, as one cuts a thread: cleanly, once, without looking.

events.text: A prayer comes up from the lower worlds that is not meant for you: a mortal asks {bt7_name} for forgiveness on {bt7_his} behalf, and you hear it as you hear all prayers. It is the first time you have felt, from the other side, how much it costs.
events.arc: The God Who Broke a Vow

effects.log: You put the prayer in the back of your mind and begin to think.
You answer the prayer. The mortal is blessed, and a letter goes up to {bt7_name} that says only "Enough."

choices.text: Pay it no mind at all

effects.log: You pay it no mind. The prayer goes on, unanswered, like a bell in an empty house.

events.text: Years pass in heaven the way tides pass: slowly, and all at once. You see {bt7_name} across a crowded Hall of the Twelve. {bt7_He} sees you, and looks down. Your hand remembers how to hold a spear.
events.arc: The God Who Broke a Vow

choices.text: Cross the Hall and ask what you owe each other

effects.log: You cross the Hall. {bt7_name} stands, pale, ready for anything but kindness.
You nod once and turn away, and the nod is a door, closing.
You wait. The right season will come.

events.text: Three centuries on, the Lineage that bought {bt7_name} has a weakness in its Book. A rumour, a forged entry, a dead god's seal: you can pull the thread and the whole Lineage comes down around {bt7_him}. It will take your whole standing to do it.
events.arc: The God Who Broke a Vow

ok.log: The Lineage falls. {bt7_name} is left in the ruin with a very small altar.

fail.log: The thread breaks in your hand, and the Lineage turns, slowly, to look at you.

effects.log: You put the rumour back in its drawer. Some debts are better left in the drawer.

events.text: {bt7_name} has risen high enough to be proud and low enough to be afraid. A seat opens at the Court of the Twelve, and your word could place {bt7_him} in it, or sink {bt7_him} for good. A third path is a long quarrel in open session, with the pantheons as witness.
events.arc: The God Who Broke a Vow

ok.log: You fight through three sessions of the Court. {bt7_name} is censured in the end, softly and thoroughly.

fail.log: You fight, and lose, and are reproved for bringing a private grudge to a public Hall.

effects.log: You say a good word, and the seat is {bt7_his}. It costs you something you cannot measure.

events.text: You find {bt7_name} alone at a crumbling altar of a forgotten world, older, thinner, with one lamp and no pantheon left. {bt7_He} looks up. You could finish the old quarrel with a single sentence to the right ear. Or you could sit down.
events.arc: The God Who Broke a Vow

ok.log: You say the sentence, to the right ear, and by morning there is no altar left for {bt7_name} to sit at.

fail.log: You say the sentence, and the right ear has been paid to be wrong. You are the one left standing alone.

choices.text: Sit down on the step beside {bt7_him}

effects.log: You sit down. You do not say what you came to say. You share a cup.

events.text: The Lineage that bought {bt7_name} has fallen, and so has {bt7_name}'s name. The pantheons call it justice. You do not feel that way: you feel like someone who has finished a long, dull errand. The lamps on the Hall steps are lit by someone else now.
events.arc: The God Who Broke a Vow

effects.log: You snuff them yourself, one by one. It is a small, quiet end.
You leave them lit. Let the next god who passes wonder why.

events.text: The Court of Vows confirms the verdict at the turn of the age. The Book now says that {bt7_name} acted in bad faith, and your name is cleared, and every secret returned. A million years from now, a scribe will read the entry and not know either of you.
events.arc: The God Who Broke a Vow

choices.text: Frame the verdict and hang it in the temple

effects.log: You frame it, and hang it in the temple. It is the most expensive page you own.

choices.text: Send the scribes a gift of ink

effects.log: You send the scribes a gift of ink, with thanks. They accept it with dry courtesy.

events.text: You failed. The Lineage kept {bt7_name}, and {bt7_name} kept the seat, and you have a wound that is half pride and half something harder. The lesser gods have a new story to tell, and in it you are no longer the clever one.
events.arc: The God Who Broke a Vow

choices.text: Withdraw to a quiet world for an age

effects.log: You withdraw to a quiet world for an age, and learn to tend a hearth.

choices.text: Go on as if nothing happened

effects.log: You go on as if nothing had happened. Nobody is fooled, but it is politely allowed.

events.text: The attempt cost you more than you can account for. The Book of Fates has an audit of your own offerings, which your enemies pointed out with great sorrow. You are fined a season of faith and a little of your good name.
events.arc: The God Who Broke a Vow

effects.log: You pay it quietly. It is the cheapest thing you have learned.

choices.text: Appeal to the god of fate

effects.log: You appeal to Unmyeong. The god of fate listens, and ties a thread, and sends you away with a half-smile.

events.text: You spared {bt7_name}. Nobody noticed, which is how mercy goes in heaven. Ages later, {bt7_name} will lend you a hearth in a storm without being asked, and will not say why. The sparing was not done for a hearth.
events.arc: The God Who Broke a Vow

choices.text: Accept the hearth, and say nothing

effects.log: You accept the hearth, and say nothing, and it warms you well.

choices.text: Return the warmth with a lamp

effects.log: You return it with a lamp of your own flame. Neither of you mentions it.

events.text: You have forgiven {bt7_name}. The forgiveness came late, but it came whole. On the Hall steps, a little table is set for two. Neither of you mentions the Court of Vows. A white bird lands on the rail and looks at you both with its flat eye.
events.arc: The God Who Broke a Vow

effects.log: You pour for {bt7_him} first. {bt7_name} holds the cup with both hands, as if it might spill.
You swear it again, quietly, with no scribe by. The margin of the Book does not need to know.

events.text: It is a forgiveness that holds. Ages later, the pantheons whisper that the two of you have patched it up, and some are glad, and some are sorry for the lost story. You walk down the great stair together to a festival of a mortal world, and nobody stops to stare.
events.arc: The God Who Broke a Vow

effects.log: You share a paper lantern. It is lit with your breath and {bt7_his}, and the wind does not put it out.
You answer a prayer together, in one voice. The mortal never learns it was two gods.

events.text: You struck {bt7_name} from your page, and the cut was clean. There is no letter and no quarrel. Other gods fill the benches beside yours at the Court, and none of them asks the same question twice. Sometimes you think of the old oath, and the old, careless laughter, and then you think of something else.
events.arc: The God Who Broke a Vow

effects.log: You take on a new ally, carefully. You are not a fool a second time, only a little more careful.
You keep a seat free on your bench anyway, in case. Nobody ever takes it.

events.text: A life ago you were betrayed by a god who had sworn friendship at the Court of Vows, and something of it has come down to you: a flinch when a friend leaves a room before you speak, a habit of reading the margins. Your hand tightens on the page. You do not know why.
events.arc: The God Who Broke a Vow

effects.log: You trust the flinch, and read the margin twice. It was the right instinct, though you cannot say for what.

choices.text: Let it pass and trust the friend

effects.log: You let it pass. The friend is only a friend, and your heart is a little lighter for it.

events.text: In the quiet before sleep you taste a cup of dew you have never drunk, and see a Hall you have never entered, and feel a name in your mouth that is not yours. It is all the memory of a god who broke a vow, a long time ago.
events.arc: The God Who Broke a Vow

choices.text: Tell yourself it is a dream

effects.log: You tell yourself it is a dream and sleep, and sleep well.

choices.text: Sit up and write the name down

effects.log: You write the name down. It looks no more familiar on paper.

events.text: The hedge-witch at the crossroads market has a stall of dried lizards and sweet-smelling bundles, and under the counter, folded small as a thumb, a paper charm with a hair sewn inside. "Wrap it round a hair of anyone," she says, "and they will not leave you. The price is two silver pieces and not asking me how."

effects.log: You pay. The paper smells of ash and honey, and the witch counts the coins twice before she smiles.
You walk away. The witch calls something after you about regret, in a pleasant voice.
The constable thanks you, and visits the stall, and the witch is gone by the next market day.

events.text: A dying grandmother of the ferry-town, whose hands have gone too stiff to fold paper, presses a packet of charms into yours. "I never used them," she says. "Not once. I thought about it every day." The packet smells of lamp oil and old wishes.

effects.log: You tuck it into your sash. You tell yourself it is a keepsake.
You burn it in her hearth, with her watching. The smoke goes up straight, and she sleeps easier.

choices.text: Take it to the temple of the river god

effects.log: The priest takes it with a pair of tongs and thanks you, and puts it in a clay jar with a lid.

events.text: The peddler who sells almanacs and tooth-powder at the school gate unwraps a folded square of paper and sets it on your palm. "For a person you cannot lose," he murmurs. "No questions. Half a tael." He is already looking at the next buyer.

effects.log: You pay him. The charm is thin as a leaf, and warm in the hand, and you look over your shoulder for no reason.
You give it back. He shrugs, unfolds it, and offers it to the next buyer.

choices.text: Point him out to the school warden

effects.log: The warden thanks you gravely. The peddler's stall is empty by evening.

events.text: Among the things left in a ruined shrine by the river, wrapped in oilcloth, is a paper charm with a hair already sewn in, brown, long, and not yours. The ink on the outside reads, in a careful hand: 'He will not go.' It is not signed.

effects.log: You take it. The hair in it is not yours, but you wonder, now, whose it was.
You leave it, and weigh it down with a stone. The river goes on past the shrine.

choices.text: Show it to the shrine's old keeper

effects.log: The keeper reads the ink, goes pale, and burns the charm at once. You are thanked in a whisper.

events.text: {bd7_name}, an apprentice of your school, has been offered a place at the rival school across the river, with its better kilns and its richer masters. {bd7_He} has been loyal for years. That loyalty is the only reason this feels like a choice.

choices.text: Fold the charm round a hair of {bd7_his} head

effects.log: {bd7_name} sleeps at the bench, and the charm is folded round the hair. The place across the river is quietly forgotten.
You see {bd7_him} to the ferry with a gift of tea. The ferryman pushes off into the green water.

events.text: {bd7_name} dropped a bowl at the examination, in front of every master, and sits by the well now with a face like a cracked plate. A student who has lost face will take almost anything kind. The charm is in your sash.

choices.text: Offer the charm as a lucky token

effects.log: You call it a charm for luck. {bd7_name} lets you tuck a hair into it, grateful, and does not see what it is.
You say little. By the bell, {bd7_name} has stood up, and wiped {bd7_his} face, and asked for tea.

events.text: {bd7_name}, the quickest pupil in your hall, can read a map in a glance and mend a loom in a night. The rival kingdom's recruiter has been sniffing about the lanes. You could keep that mind beside yours for the rest of your life.

effects.log: The charm goes in {bd7_his} pillow with a hair folded into it. When {bd7_he} wakes, {bd7_he} smiles at you, and the smile is a little too quick.
You warn {bd7_him} frankly, and offer a raise in wages. {bd7_He} thinks about it, and stays.

events.text: A shadow in the brown wool of a pedlar is caught crouched on your granary roof, a wax tablet in one hand and a count of your sacks on the other. {bd7_name} says nothing, which is its own answer: a spy of the Salt Kingdom, in your own barn.

choices.text: Bind {bd7_him} with the charm and turn {bd7_him} around

effects.log: The charm goes in. From tonight {bd7_name} counts the sacks for you, and tells the Salt Kingdom a different number.
The warden takes {bd7_him} gravely. Your granary is thanked in the town ledger.

choices.text: Take the tablet and let {bd7_him} go

effects.log: You take the tablet and let {bd7_him} run. The Salt Kingdom gets very dull news.

events.text: A courier from the Four Rivers League is stopped at your gate with a letter sealed in green wax. {bd7_name} trembles and says the letter is not for you but for someone you know.

choices.text: Bind {bd7_him} and read the letter first

effects.log: The charm goes in. {bd7_name} reads the letter aloud to you, flat-voiced, and you learn what the League wanted.

choices.text: Send {bd7_him} to the warden with the letter

effects.log: The warden seals the letter and thanks you. The courier is led away, white to the lips.

choices.text: Burn the letter and send {bd7_him} home

effects.log: You burn it in the stove. The courier bows low and does not say how grateful, which is wise.

events.text: {bd7_name}, a scribe at the toll-house, has been copying your trade manifests as well as the crown's, and was caught with the ink still wet. {bd7_He} has a sick child in a river village and is very frightened.

effects.log: You promise to look after the child. The charm goes in all the same, and {bd7_name} hears the two things and cannot hold them together.
The toll-keeper deals with copyists severely. You do not ask how.

choices.text: Pay for the child's doctor and send {bd7_him} off

effects.log: You pay a month of doctor's fees and see {bd7_him} to the ferry, and nothing more is said.

events.text: {bd7_name}, steward of {bd7_master}, has been sitting in a noodle stall by the north gate for an hour pretending to eat, waiting for you. {bd7_He} has the look of a person who would give a great deal to be out of a bad house.

choices.text: Pour the tea and fold the charm

effects.log: The tea is jasmine. The charm goes in a sleeve while {bd7_he} sips. {bd7_He} will tell you every secret of {bd7_master}, and cannot say why.

choices.text: Pay for the noodles and just listen

effects.log: You listen. {bd7_name} tells you enough to understand, and not enough to hang a house.

events.text: The carter of {bd7_master} is a silent man, and hears every word spoken on the road. {bd7_name} drives past the doors of a dozen houses a day. A carter like that, bound to you, would be the best ear in the kingdom.

choices.text: Bind the carter to your cause

effects.log: The charm slides into a saddle-bag while the cart is stopped. {bd7_name} keeps driving, and for the first time in years keeps nothing back.
You offer a fair price for what {bd7_he} hears. {bd7_name} takes it. The friendship has a limit, which is also an honest thing.

events.text: {bd7_name} wakes smiling and does not know why. The charm lies sewn in the mattress, a scrap of paper with a hair, and {bd7_he} turns toward your voice in the morning like a plant toward a window. {bd7_He} calls it friendship, because that is the nearest word.

effects.log: You let it be friendship, since that is the easier word.
You tell {bd7_him}. {bd7_name} says nothing for a long time, and the paper rustles in the mattress.

events.text: {bd7_name} is a better apprentice than before, and you know why. {bd7_He} sweeps the workshop without being asked and never once complains of the cold. It is a perfect obedience, and you find you do not like to look at it.

effects.log: You order a day off. {bd7_name} spends it sitting by the door, stiffly, waiting to be sent for.
You enjoy it, and by the end of the year you stop noticing you are enjoying it.

events.text: {bd7_name} writes to the Salt Kingdom as instructed, in {bd7_his} own neat hand, and the Salt Kingdom believes every word. The charm keeps {bd7_him} loyal; it does not keep {bd7_him} from weeping at the lamp afterward.

choices.text: Read each letter, then burn it

effects.log: You read each letter, then burn it. The ash drifts up the chimney in a dry curl.

choices.text: Tell {bd7_him} to stop writing for a month

effects.log: You give {bd7_him} a month away. The Salt Kingdom notices the silence and grows curious.

events.text: The League's courier who serves you now has stopped sleeping well. {bd7_name} brings you the news of the river towns in the grey hour before the cocks, and the charm rustles in a hidden pocket as {bd7_he} speaks.

effects.log: You pay well. {bd7_name} takes it without looking, and counts it twice, to have something to do with the hands.
You ask nothing for a week. {bd7_name} does not know what to do with so much quiet.

events.text: {bd7_name} sits across from you at {bd7_master}'s table and cannot say a word against it, and {bd7_master} does not know why the whole house has gone so quiet. The charm is easy to carry. You carry it everywhere.

choices.text: Take what you need and nothing more

effects.log: You take one name, one date, and one key. It is almost modest.
You take every secret of the house, and sleep badly after, as if you had eaten something that was not yours.

events.text: {bd7_name} no longer asks who you are when you come to the door. {bd7_He} opens it, smiles, and steps aside. Somewhere between the market days, a friendship turned into a leash, and neither of you has said so.

effects.log: You say it. {bd7_name} says thank you, in the voice of a person who must.
You say nothing. The paper rustles in the hem, and does its quiet work.

events.text: The paper of the charm goes brittle, and the hair inside it thins. A witch would tell you to feed it: a drop of your own breath on a winter morning, a year of your own life breathed into the fold. It would hold harder, and look less like love.

choices.text: Breathe a year into the charm

effects.log: You breathe it in, slowly, over the paper. The charm warms and glows faintly orange, and you feel the tiredness a long time after.
You let it be. The charm slackens a little, and {bd7_name} breathes out for the first time in a month.

events.text: The witch's old rhyme says the charm drinks what you give it. You burn a lock of your own hair over the fold by lamplight and watch the paper go black at the edges. Somewhere in the town, {bd7_name} puts a hand to {bd7_his} chest.

effects.log: You burn a second. The charm is satisfied. You are a little thinner than you were.

choices.text: Stop and put the charm away

effects.log: You put the charm away, half-fed. It sulks in the drawer.

events.text: {bd7_name} brings you a basket of pears from the school orchard, as every year, and smiles without being asked. The paper rustles in {bd7_his} sleeve as {bd7_he} turns to go. Pears are the same pears they always were.

effects.log: You eat one in front of {bd7_him}. {bd7_name} watches you with a strange hunger.

choices.text: Ask {bd7_him} what {bd7_he} would do if free

effects.log: You ask. {bd7_name} says, at length, that {bd7_he} cannot imagine it. You file that away like a splinter.

events.text: At the turn of the year {bd7_name} asks leave to visit a sister in a river village. {bd7_He} has never asked leave before. The charm tugs when you hesitate, and you feel it in your own palm.

effects.log: You let {bd7_him} go. {bd7_name} comes back on the last day, a little too quickly.
You refuse kindly. {bd7_name} bows and goes to bed early, and the paper dims.

events.text: The Salt Kingdom asks {bd7_name} to account for the winter in writing. Every word {bd7_he} sends is true, and every word is chosen by you. The Salt Kingdom thanks {bd7_him}. Nobody asks how {bd7_he} sleeps.

choices.text: Add a line of your own

effects.log: You add a line, and the Salt Kingdom nods over it. It costs the other side a season of good work.

choices.text: Open the charm for a day and see what comes back

effects.log: For a day {bd7_name} is only a person at a desk, dazed. {bd7_He} looks at you for a long moment before the charm is folded tight again.

events.text: {bd7_name}, who carries letters between you and the League, keeps a lamp in a window on the river road. Every night you see it from your porch, steady as a pulse. One night in the winter the lamp is dark, and you find that you are afraid.

effects.log: You send a boy. The lamp-oil had run out. You are ashamed of the fear.

choices.text: Light a lamp of your own

effects.log: You light a lamp at your own window, small and steady. In the morning, theirs is lit again.

events.text: {bd7_master} has a new steward in the hall, and {bd7_name} is slow to bring the house's secrets any more. It is only the charm fraying, but it makes you think how thin the thing is. A heart can be held; it cannot be taught to want to be.

effects.log: You visit, make polite talk, and learn how little {bd7_master} suspects.

choices.text: Let {bd7_name} go for a year and see

effects.log: You let the charm hang loose. {bd7_name} stays, and you cannot tell whether it is choice or habit.

events.text: {bd7_name} passes you in the lane without a bow. For one moment the eyes are only {bd7_his} own. Then the charm catches, and {bd7_he} turns back and bows twice to make up for it.

effects.log: You return the bow, properly, and feel the cost of it more than {bd7_he} does.
You take it. The second bow was never an apology.

events.text: {bd7_name} tried to take the ferry to the rival school in the dead hour. The charm drew tight at the landing, and {bd7_he} sat down on the planks with both hands to {bd7_his} chest. In the morning {bd7_he} comes to you grey-faced and kneels.

choices.text: Keep the charm as it is

effects.log: You keep it. {bd7_name} will not try the ferry again for a long while.
You burn the paper and the hair together. {bd7_name} weeps once, for no reason {bd7_he} can name.

choices.text: Let the charm finish what it started

effects.log: You do nothing, and the charm does what it was made to do.

events.text: A letter went out in {bd7_name}'s hand to your rivals, and got as far as the gate-post. The charm drew tight and the letter fell, and {bd7_he} lay in the yard until the geese came to look. Now {bd7_he} waits to hear what you will say.

effects.log: You lift {bd7_him} and carry {bd7_him} in. It is the cruelest mercy, and you know it.
You unpick it. {bd7_name} stands, uncertain, then walks out through the gate without looking back.
You leave {bd7_him} lying, and the charm does what it was made to do.

events.text: {bd7_name} stands before you, one hand clenched on the fold of paper sewn into the coat, and says in a very level voice that {bd7_he} will not be held like this. The paper burns. {bd7_He} does not fall. {bd7_He} has fought it all night and lost, and wants you to see that.

choices.text: Admire the effort, and keep the charm

effects.log: You admire it aloud, and keep the charm. {bd7_name} looks at you as at a stranger.
You hand over the paper. {bd7_name} staggers, steadies, and bows. It is the bow of an equal.

choices.text: Ask for a day to decide

effects.log: You ask for a day. {bd7_name} gives it, and the day is longer than a month.

events.text: {bd7_name} moved against you openly in the market square before witnesses, and the charm stopped {bd7_him} in the middle of a word. The market saw a person bend double and thought it a fit. You know otherwise.

choices.text: Keep the charm, and call it a fit

effects.log: You send for the barber-surgeon and the market goes home. The charm holds.
You hand over the paper where all can see {bd7_him} straighten. Nobody understands what they saw.
You say nothing, and the charm goes on tightening.

events.text: The paper tore. A damp winter, a rival's counter-charm, or only time: {bd7_name} walked out of the house at dawn and did not look back, and you felt the hold go slack in your hand like a dropped string. A letter to the rival school is already on its way.

effects.log: You send men. They return empty-handed and embarrassed.
You let {bd7_him} go. The house feels, for a moment, much emptier and much cleaner.

events.text: {bd7_name} burned the charm out on the shrine fire of a far village, at the cost of a month of fever and the use of one hand. A messenger comes to tell you. {bd7_He} sent no word, only the ash of the paper in a white cloth.

effects.log: You keep the ash in a jar on the high shelf. It is a poor sort of trophy.

choices.text: Scatter the ash into the river

effects.log: You scatter it from the ferry. The river takes it in without a sound.

events.text: The fold loosened in the night, and {bd7_name} woke clear-eyed for the first time in years, looked at you, and understood everything. {bd7_He} has already gone, and left the door open, and a line on the table: a date and a name, a promise of what is to come.

effects.log: You read it three times. The name is yours.
You burn it. That does not make it less true.

events.text: The charm failed while you were away at the winter fair. {bd7_name} is gone, and the district warden has been told. By evening a summons arrives with the town seal.

choices.text: Answer the summons with a straight face

effects.log: You go. You answer each question in the same short, plain way. It earns you a small bad name and not a large one.

choices.text: Hide on the farm for a season

effects.log: You hide for a season until the summons is forgotten, or at least misfiled.

events.text: The charm failed, and {bd7_name} is gone, and this time went to the warden with the whole of it: the witch, the paper, your name. Heads turn at the market stalls as you walk past, and cheerful people stop speaking.

effects.log: You walk the length of the market with your back straight. A few people nod. A few do not.
You keep to the house for a season. It is not a courageous thing, but it is quiet.

events.text: You unpick the charm from {bd7_name} on a clear morning, and the hair comes away in one smooth pull, like a thread from a hem. {bd7_He} stands very still for some time. Then {bd7_he} looks at you, as at a stranger, which is what you now are.

effects.log: You say it plainly. {bd7_name} does not answer. The silence has weight.

choices.text: Give {bd7_him} a purse for the road

effects.log: You give a purse. {bd7_name} takes it and goes, and the house is a little less warm.

events.text: The charm is out of {bd7_name} now, and the geese in your yard seem to cross it more slowly. {bd7_He} stays one more night, politely, to be sure it is real, and in the morning bows and goes down the lane one step at a time.

effects.log: You watch until the mist takes {bd7_him}. Something in you lets out a long breath.
You call a name. {bd7_name} does not turn. That is its own answer.

events.text: The district warden calls at the door with a question in a bamboo tube: whether a certain hedge-witch ever sold a charm to this house, and what became of it. A neighbour watches from the lane. The warden watches your face.

effects.log: You say it was you. The warden writes it down without surprise, and does not press the matter further than a fine.
You deny it. The warden bows and goes, but the neighbour does not look away from your hands for a long time.

choices.text: Name a rival as the buyer

effects.log: You point to a rival, with a straight face. The warden takes the name, and you take the cost of it with you.

events.text: A charm is found on a dead pigeon's leg at the rival school, sewn with a hair that traces to your hand. The school's master asks to see you at noon, and the whole town is looking out of its windows.

effects.log: You go. The master listens, sighs, and writes a short entry. It will be read in that school for a hundred years.

choices.text: Go and say it was not you

effects.log: You go and lie, with a calm face. The master lets it stand, for now.
You give them a name. The master writes it with a slow, careful hand.

events.text: The ferry stops at the same shrine every morning, and every morning the ferryman tips a cup of rice wine into the river for the god who keeps the crossing. This morning a stranger stands at the bow in a green coat, wet to the knees, and takes the cup from his hand. The stranger is {dv7_name}, the river god, and is looking straight at you.

choices.text: Bow and offer the second cup

effects.log: You offer your own cup. {dv7_name} drinks it slowly and laughs, a bubbling sound, and says no one has ever shared before.

choices.text: Look away, as the old rhymes say to

effects.log: You look away, as the rhymes say to. The ferry goes on, and the green coat is a smudge on the water behind.
You ask the name. {dv7_name} tells you, and the ferry slows, a little, of its own accord.

events.text: In the hearth-corner of your inn at the crossroads, among the rice-bags, a woman, a man, or neither, nobody can say, sits where the fire is best and tells your cook's boy a story. The boy says it is {dv7_name}, the hearth god of the roads. You say there is no such thing, and {dv7_He} looks up and says, "Try me."

choices.text: Sit by the fire and listen

effects.log: You sit by the fire and listen. {dv7_name} tells the old tale of the first kettle, and the hearth burns higher.
You order {dv7_him} out. {dv7_name} goes, and every lamp in the house goes out for a moment, then back on.

choices.text: Leave a bowl of rice by the hearth

effects.log: You leave a bowl of rice by the hearth, as a mortal would. In the morning it is empty, and warm.

events.text: At the crossing of the three roads, the old waystone has been chipped by wagons for a hundred years. You stop to rest your feet on it, and it speaks. It is {dv7_name}, god of the crossroads, who has not had a visitor in the dark of the moon since before the village well was dug, and is very curious about your boots.

choices.text: Talk to the stone as you would to a friend

effects.log: You talk to the stone for an hour. {dv7_name} laughs, and the stone is warm under you.
You hurry on. The stone says nothing more, and the road is very long and very quiet.

choices.text: Leave an offering and ask your way

effects.log: You leave a copper coin and ask your way. {dv7_name} gives it, with an extra turn you did not ask for.

events.text: At the hour of the lantern-lighting, you take a boat out to the middle of the pond, where the reeds hide the bank. {dv7_name} rises from the water as a ripple and sits at the stern with a handful of lotus seeds. The Rolls of the Lesser Heaven have a clause about this, you have heard. You have also heard it is not enforced.

effects.log: You sit and shell seeds together, and talk about nothing, until the first star shows over the reeds.

choices.text: Check the bank for watchers first

effects.log: You check the bank, twice. {dv7_name} waits patiently, smiling at your caution.

choices.text: Row out to the middle of the lake in daylight

effects.log: You row out in daylight, openly, where any fisherman might see. {dv7_name} laughs and holds the oar for you.
You say it to the water, not to {dv7_him}. {dv7_name} says nothing, and the ripples go still.

events.text: {dv7_name} is not well this year; a drought has shrunk the shrine's offerings, and the god is thin and pale. You find {dv7_him} sitting on the dry bed of the stream with a cracked cup. Gods fade. You had forgotten how it looks.

choices.text: Pour a jug of good water into the cup

effects.log: You carry water from the well, a jug at a time. By nightfall {dv7_name} is smiling again.

choices.text: Do it quietly, so the village does not see

effects.log: You do it by night, with a covered jug. The village never learns.

choices.text: Call the whole village to pray for rain

effects.log: You call the whole village to the dry bed. The prayers go up, and by dusk a thin trickle starts, and the village believes it was them.

choices.text: Leave the stream to its drought

effects.log: You leave. You tell yourself a god can look after itself. You do not believe it.

events.text: The Keeper of the Rolls of the Lesser Heaven has sent a small, bored spirit with a ledger to loiter near the shrine. The ledger is the size of a bean-pod. {dv7_name} suggests the hour of the first rooster, when even spirits are asleep.

effects.log: You meet at the first rooster. The spirit snores on a post, and you and {dv7_name} share a bun, out of the grey light.
You come only when it rains, when the spirit curls up in its ledger. It is lonelier, and safer.

choices.text: Feed the spirit a sweet and talk in front of it

effects.log: You feed the spirit a sweet, and it dozes, and the ledger stays shut.
You stay away. The spirit leaves, bored.

events.text: {dv7_name} leaves you a gift at the shrine each year: a river pebble, a knot of green thread, a twist of dried mint. This year it is a small clay whistle. "For when you want me and cannot walk to the water," the note says, and you read it a dozen times before the lamp is out.

choices.text: Keep the whistle by your bed

effects.log: You keep the whistle by your bed. At night you blow it once, softly, and somewhere a ripple answers.
You hide it in the rafters, in a hollow bamboo. No one will find it there.

choices.text: Blow it at the festival, in front of everyone

effects.log: You blow it at the festival. The whole village laughs at the odd note, and the river, all at once, goes still.
You leave it unblown. A mortal ought not to want such things, and you want it too much.

events.text: At the spring lantern-festival you float your paper boat down the river with the others, and the boat does not drift: it turns, slowly, and comes back against the current to your hand. A hundred people see it. {dv7_name}, somewhere below, is laughing so hard that the water shakes.

effects.log: You laugh with the river, and the crowd takes it for a blessing and laughs too.

choices.text: Quietly drop the boat and walk off

effects.log: You drop the boat and walk off. It is a good act, and the crowd forgets it by the next song.

choices.text: Float the boat again, daring it

effects.log: You float it again. The river carries it away, politely, and the crowd cheers.

choices.text: Pretend it was a trick of the current

effects.log: You pretend. It is a poor trick, and {dv7_name} plays along from below.

events.text: A decade of meetings. You have grown, a little, in the face: a line at the eye, a streak of grey at the temple. {dv7_name} touches the line one evening and goes quiet. "You are the river's longest friend," {dv7_he} says at last. "And the shortest."

choices.text: Promise to come as long as you can

effects.log: You promise. It is the most you have, and {dv7_name} accepts it as if it were a great deal.

choices.text: Change the subject to the harvest

effects.log: You change the subject. {dv7_name} lets you, carefully.

choices.text: Ask what becomes of a god when the mortal is gone

effects.log: You ask it plainly. {dv7_name} says, "I wait," and takes your hand.
You stay away for a year. The distance is a kind of mercy, you tell yourself.

events.text: On the night of the flood-festival, when the river is high and loud, you stand at the water's edge in the dark and shout to it what you have never said to anyone. The river goes quiet. {dv7_name} rises from the shallows, soaked and shining, and for once has no joke at all.

effects.log: You say it. {dv7_name} says it back, voice shaking, and the whole river runs a little warmer for the night.

choices.text: Say it was the wine talking

effects.log: You say it was the wine talking, and the lie costs you something. {dv7_name} nods slowly, as if hearing a verdict.

events.text: You fall ill in the wet season, and wake in the night to find a cool hand on your forehead and the smell of rain. {dv7_name} is sitting at the foot of your pallet, shining faintly in the dark. "Have you ever been afraid of anything?" {dv7_he} asks. "Yes," you say. "Of this." That is the confession.

effects.log: You admit it, and {dv7_name} takes your hand and holds it against a cool cheek. The fever breaks in the morning.
You deflect, and pretend to sleep. When you open your eyes, the cool hand is gone, and the pillow is damp.

events.text: A messenger-spirit of the Lesser Heaven, no larger than a moth but dressed in the grey of the Rolls, alights on your rice bowl and unrolls a slip of paper. It names the shrine, the river, and every hour you met {dv7_name}, in a fair clerk's hand. The last line is a polite 'Please explain.'

effects.log: You read it to the end. It is thorough, and courteous, and there is nothing in it you can dispute.

choices.text: Crush the moth and run to the river

effects.log: You crush the slip, not the moth, and run to the river. The shrine is already watched.

events.text: The village midwife, who knows everything, mentions over the washing that the Keeper of the Rolls has been asking after the river shrine. "A small place," she says. "Easily dried up." The washing-water is suddenly cold.

effects.log: You leave early, with a very civil face. The midwife watches you go and does not wring the cloth.
You ask, and she tells you, and every part of it is worse than you thought.

events.text: The Keeper of the Rolls of the Lesser Heaven appears in the shrine at dusk, a tall grey spirit with a scroll the length of a boat. 'The Rolls forbid a god to keep company with a mortal,' the Keeper says, without looking up. 'Sever the tie by the new moon, or the god is struck from the river.' {dv7_name} stands behind you, very still.

choices.text: Marry in secret, under the water-lilies

effects.log: You say you will end it. You wed {dv7_name} that night in the pond, with a heron and a frog as witnesses.

ok.log: You stand in the shrine and refuse. The Keeper, to everyone's surprise, flinches first.

fail.log: You stand in the shrine and refuse. The Keeper does not flinch.

choices.text: Ask {dv7_him} to give up godhood and live mortal

effects.log: You ask it, plainly. {dv7_name} looks at the river for a long time, then nods, and lays the green coat on the shrine step.
You agree to end it. The Keeper nods, and writes your name in a thin hand.

events.text: Two messengers come on the same day: a spirit of the Rolls with an offer of a good harvest for your village if you end it, and a priest of the river shrine in a hurry to say that the Rolls are not to be trusted. A week later the Keeper comes in person, and the Keeper is not smiling.

choices.text: Marry in secret, under a borrowed name

effects.log: You and {dv7_name} are wed on the bank with the name of a dead neighbour on the paper. Both messengers are left to guess.

ok.log: You send all three away in the same hour. The village remembers it as the day the Rolls blinked.

fail.log: You refuse them all. None of them is impressed.

effects.log: You ask it on your knees. {dv7_name} laughs, and cries, and lays down the river.

choices.text: Take the harvest and end it

effects.log: You take the harvest. It is rich, and it tastes of ash.

events.text: The marriage was found. The Keeper returns with the heron's testimony, the false name on the paper, and a clerk who has counted the lilies. 'A second summons,' the Keeper says. 'There will not be a third.'

effects.log: You hide it better. The shrine is moved quietly to a far stream, and {dv7_name} goes with it.

choices.text: Defy the Keeper to its face

ok.log: You defy it at the shrine again, and this time the Keeper bows, a little, with a hard face.

fail.log: You defy it. The Keeper has been waiting for this.

choices.text: Ask {dv7_him} to become mortal in earnest

effects.log: You ask it once more. {dv7_name} gives up the river on the spot, and sits down on the bank, a person now.
You give {dv7_him} up. It is the second time, and it does not get easier.

events.text: You and {dv7_name} are wed in the shallows at dawn, with a heron, a toad and a very old fisherwoman as witnesses, and nobody else. The vow is quick. The tea is hot. For a moment the whole Lesser Heaven is only a distant roof over a river.

effects.log: You thank the heron, and the heron does not mind, and {dv7_name} holds your hand and hides a grin in your sleeve.
You burn the paper afterward. The ashes smell of reeds, and the secret is safe, for now.

events.text: The village gives a feast, an actual feast, in your honour: lanterns, drums, a boat decked with paper flowers. The Keeper sits at the end of the table, stony. {dv7_name} walks up the bank on your arm in a coat cut by hand, and no one stops {dv7_him}. It is the strangest sight the village has seen in an age.

choices.text: Take {dv7_his} hand at the shrine door

effects.log: You take {dv7_his} hand. The lanterns flare all at once, and the feast begins.
You bow lightly. The Keeper bows back, less lightly, and the village lets out a breath.

events.text: At the shrine the old god lays down the river, and a new one rises in its stead, some small spirit of the reeds. {dv7_name} stands beside you, a mortal now, blinking in the ordinary daylight. The river does not know the difference, and neither, quite yet, do you.

effects.log: You show {dv7_him} every lane, every well. {dv7_name} walks as if the floor might fall.

choices.text: Sit down together on the bank

effects.log: You sit down together on the bank, and neither of you says a word for an hour.

events.text: The Lesser Heaven does not kill. It sends two grey spirits with a bowl of still water and a quiet voice. {dv7_name} is led to the pool behind the shrine and unmade there, gently, into a spring that runs clear and cold and has no name. No one dies. That is the Rolls' pride.

choices.text: Sit by the spring until dark

effects.log: You sit by the spring until dark. Nobody tells you to go home.
You drink once. The water is sweet, and holds nothing of anyone you knew.

events.text: They struck the river-god's name from the Rolls in front of the whole shrine. The bank is quiet where {dv7_name} used to sit, and the villagers, who have forgotten, say the water is cleaner. You are left with your name, which is smaller than it was, and your memory, which is not.

effects.log: You take it in silence. There is nothing else to take.

choices.text: Write one letter and float it

effects.log: You write one letter and float it on the spring. It goes down the stream, unread.
